title: Telephone Triage Boundaries and Avoiding Medical Advice

sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain what telephone triage is and identify which professionals may perform clinical triage.
- Recognize the medical office assistant's boundaries regarding medical advice, diagnosis, and medication instructions.
- Escalate concerning symptoms and potential emergencies promptly to licensed clinicians.
- Recognize common emergency and red-flag presentations that require immediate emergency activation.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Triage is like a busy restaurant host who figures out which guest needs help right now and which one can wait comfortably, instead of seating people only in the order they walked in.

### Question 2

Deciding how sick someone is and what help they need is the medic's job — like how the trained lifeguard, not the person selling tickets, decides who needs rescuing.

### Question 3

The assistant is like a message runner who writes down exactly what the caller says and hands it to the right helper, rather than being the one who makes the big decision.

### Question 4

A lifeguard's helper can run and get the lifeguard, but they should not jump in and decide who can swim without the training to make that call.

### Question 5

Telling someone to stop their medicine is like telling them to take off their safety gear — only the expert in charge gets to make that decision.

### Question 6

It is like saying "I'll ask the grown-up" instead of guessing an answer when you are not the one trained to decide.

### Question 7

It is like a sous chef who preps ingredients and helps the head chef, but the head chef decides the recipe.

### Question 8

You hand the note to the doctor or nurse — not to the person at the cash register or a relative guessing.

### Question 9

A red flag is like a fire alarm — when it goes off, you stop what you are doing and get help fast.

### Question 10

It is like calling for an ambulance right away instead of telling someone who is badly hurt to just wait it out.

### Question 11

Crushing chest pain is like a smoke alarm going off — you act right now, not later.

### Question 12

A patient's health information is like a private diary — only the people who are helping with their care get to peek inside.

### Question 13

It is like writing down every clue at a scene so the detective has everything they need to solve it.

### Question 14

Urgent is like a flat tire you fix right away; non-urgent is like a squeaky door that can wait a bit.

### Question 15

Your scope is like your list of approved chores — you stick to your list even when things get busy.

### Question 16

Booking an appointment or passing along a note is safe to do; deciding about medicines or illnesses is not.

### Question 17

Only the trained professional — the doctor or nurse — gets to give medical advice, like only the lifeguard gives swimming advice.

### Question 18

Follow the playbook the team wrote together, and when you are not sure, ask the coach instead of guessing.

### Question 19

Protocols are like the office playbook everyone agrees on so no one has to invent answers on the spot.

### Question 20

Lab results are like a tricky report card — the teacher, not the front desk, explains what it means.

### Question 21

Saying "you'll be fine" is guessing when you are not the one trained to check — and guessing wrong could hurt someone.

### Question 22

When you do not know the answer, pass the note to the person who does instead of making something up.

### Question 23

The safe answer points the person to the expert rather than guessing from your own experience.

### Question 24

Write down exactly what the person said, like a reporter taking careful notes, instead of adding your own guess.

### Question 25

Refilling medicine is the doctor's job — the assistant hands the request to the right person instead of signing off on it.

### Question 26

Before sharing a secret, you check that you are really talking to the right person.

### Question 27

The assistant collects the clues and hands them to the expert; they do not solve the case themselves.

### Question 28

It is like driving a car without a driver's license — doing something only licensed people are allowed to do.

### Question 29

A headache this sudden and severe is like a warning siren that needs a fast response, not a nap.

### Question 30

Trouble breathing is like a car running out of air — you do not wait, you get help now.

### Question 31

These signs are like a red fire alarm for the brain — call for help right away, do not wait to see what happens.

### Question 32

Swelling that makes it hard to swallow is like a door closing on the airway — get emergency help now.

### Question 33

Blood thinners are powerful medicine — only the doctor decides when to pause them, not the front desk.

### Question 34

Deciding about antibiotics is the doctor's job — the assistant passes the question along instead of answering it.

### Question 35

When someone guesses their own illness from the internet, the assistant hands the question to the doctor instead of saying yes or no.

### Question 36

After surgery, changes at the incision are for the doctor to check, not for the assistant to call normal.

### Question 37

When someone asks for your opinion on their health, the safe move is to point them to the expert, not to share your own guess.

### Question 38

A new rash from medicine is a warning sign — write it down and tell the doctor, do not decide what to do yourself.

### Question 39

Insulin is like a precise balance scale — only the doctor adjusts the weights, never the front desk.

### Question 40

Bleeding during pregnancy is a sign to get the doctor involved right away, not to guess it is fine.

### Question 41

After a hit to the head, confusion and vomiting mean get emergency help now, not a nap.

### Question 42

Babies' medicine is extra tricky, so the assistant hands the question to the expert instead of guessing a dose.

### Question 43

Even when someone says they do not want to bother anyone, chest pressure is a fire alarm — you still sound it.

### Question 44

Changing how much medicine someone takes is the doctor's decision, even when the reason is cost.

### Question 45

Only the doctor can write a prescription for their own patient — the assistant politely says no and explains why.

### Question 46

A very high fever that is not going away is a signal to get the doctor involved now.

### Question 47

If someone talks about hurting themselves, that is a code-red — get them to someone who can help right now.

### Question 48

Figuring out whether medicine caused a symptom is the doctor's job — the assistant writes it down and passes it along.

### Question 49

When someone speaks another language, get a translator so nothing important gets lost, then get help.

### Question 50

Stay calm like a steady anchor, listen, and pass the concern to the right person instead of fighting back.

### Question 51

Follow the team's playbook, and when the playbook is unclear, ask the coach instead of making up a new play.

### Question 52

Checking a mole for cancer is the doctor's job — the assistant books the appointment instead of guessing.

### Question 53

Severe belly pain with a hard belly is a get-help-now sign, not a wait-and-see.

### Question 54

Do not tell someone to stop their medicine because of something they read — get the doctor to look at it first.

### Question 55

The person with chest pain and trouble breathing goes to the front of the line, like the most urgent emergency.

### Question 56

Reading an X-ray report is the doctor's job — the assistant hands it over instead of explaining it.

### Question 57

When you are not sure, ask the expert instead of guessing it is fine — better safe than sorry.

### Question 58

How much of a vitamin someone should take is for the expert to say, not a guess from the front desk.

### Question 59

Do not change blood pressure medicine on a guess — get the doctor to decide, and quickly.

### Question 60

The boundary is like a fence — you stay on your side by helping connect the caller, not by handing out medical answers.

### Question 61

Checking whether two medicines clash is a job for the pharmacist or doctor, not a guess at the desk.

### Question 62

A cut that keeps bleeding needs help now, not a bandage and a wish.

### Question 63

The assistant cannot say for sure what germ someone has — that is for the test and the doctor to decide.

### Question 64

A patient's health details are private — you do not share them with a boss or anyone else unless the patient says it is okay.

### Question 65

When a test comes back abnormal, the doctor explains it — the assistant sets up that conversation.

### Question 66

When you are not sure how serious something is, ask the expert — better to pass it up than to guess wrong.

### Question 67

Kids' medicine doses need an expert — the assistant passes the question to the pharmacist or doctor.

### Question 68

Only a written, doctor-approved instruction lets the assistant help with a dose change — otherwise it goes to the doctor.

### Question 69

Fainting is a clue that something might be wrong — get the doctor to check it out soon.

### Question 70

A possible broken bone needs a doctor to look at it, not a wait-and-see at home.

### Question 71

The person who suddenly cannot see goes first, like the most serious emergency jumps the line.

### Question 72

Even if someone calls it heartburn, chest pressure reaching the jaw and arm is a fire alarm — call for help.

### Question 73

Picking someone's medicine for them is like acting as their doctor without a license — that is the line you must not cross.

### Question 74

A baby who is extra sleepy with a weak cry and poor feeding needs a doctor quickly, not a reassurance.

### Question 75

Saying "it's probably nothing" is guessing, and guessing wrong can make someone wait too long to get help.

### Question 76

Even when someone says it is just something they ate, chest discomfort is worth checking with the doctor.

### Question 77

Booking an appointment is on the assistant's chore list; deciding emergencies, medicines, and test results is not.

### Question 78

A terrible headache with a stiff neck and fever is a red flag that needs a doctor fast.

### Question 79

When you are not sure whether someone needs the hospital, ask the expert instead of guessing yes or no.

### Question 80

Face drooping, weak arm, and slurred speech together mean call for an ambulance right now.

### Question 81

Write down exactly what the patient said and hand it to the doctor, without cheering on or blocking their decision.

### Question 82

Coughing up blood is a get-help-now sign, not a sip-of-water-and-wait situation.

### Question 83

Share health details only with the people actually helping with care, like giving a key only to the people who need in.

### Question 84

One swollen, painful leg in someone who has had clots is a warning sign to get the doctor involved fast.

### Question 85

Even when someone pushes for an answer, the safe move is to say you cannot diagnose and hand them to the doctor.

### Question 86

Chest tightness, lightheadedness, and sweating after effort are alarms, not something to snack through.

### Question 87

Trouble breathing that keeps getting worse is a now-or-never emergency, not a tomorrow appointment.

### Question 88

A headache after a fall is a big deal — get the doctor to check it, not a nap.

### Question 89

A protocol is like following a written recipe from the chef; giving advice is inventing your own dish and serving it.

### Question 90

A sudden tearing pain in the chest going to the back is a mayday — call for help now.
